column4: The ayah explicitly makes طَغَا physical: when the water overflowed, God carried humanity in the vessel; it is the section's flood sense of transgression and its saving barrier in one scene.
Valleys run according to their measure while the torrent bears rising foam; the foam passes and what benefits people remains, giving the section's moral overflow a precise water-and-truth analogue.
When the people of Saba turn away, the flood of the dam, سَيْلَ الْعَرِمِ, is sent against their gardens; a breached water barrier becomes the outward answer to an inward turning-away.
The two bodies of water are released to meet, staging the water whose motion requires a boundary.
Between the two waters stands a barrier and neither تجاوزes it, لَا يَبْغِيَانِ; this is the section's dam restraining overflow in literal form, completed by 55:19.
The earth is made to burst as springs, وَفَجَّرْنَا الْأَرْضَ عُيُونًا, and the waters meet for a measured decree; the physical فجر image becomes the Flood's appointed punishment.
The people are drowned because of their sins, مِمَّا خَطِيئَاتِهِمْ أُغْرِقُوا, making moral wrongdoing and engulfing water explicitly causal.
Allah dislikes the hypocrites' اِنْبِعَاث and holds them back; divine restraint acts as a dam against a harmful setting-out, the reverse of Thamud's worst man surging forward.

Had they gone out, they would have rushed among the believers seeking discord and found listeners; it explains in social terms why their launch is restrained in 9:46 and how one impulse can spread through a group.
The human being wants لِيَفْجُرَ أَمَامَهُ, to keep breaking out into sin ahead of him; it directly names the inward fujur that the section pictures as released water.
His question about when Resurrection will be clarifies 75:5: the forward burst of sin depends on pushing away the reckoning that would bound it.
إِنَّ الْإِنسَانَ لَيَطْغَى states the section's claim in its broadest form: the human being himself overflows his proper limit.
أَن رَّآهُ اسْتَغْنَى names the pressure behind the overflow in 96:6: seeing oneself as self-sufficient removes the felt need for a restraint.
God sends Moses to Pharaoh with the diagnosis إِنَّهُ طَغَى; this is the same transgression as Thamud's, addressed before its punishment arrives.
Moses offers Pharaoh purification, أَن تَزَكَّى, placing cultivated growth against the overflow named in 79:17 just as the section opposes fujur to the soul's protection and purification.
فَأَمَّا مَن طَغَى opens one of the two outcomes with the very act of overflowing the limit.
Preferring the nearer life specifies what the transgressor of 79:37 lets carry him away.
Hell becomes the abode of the one described in 79:37-38, so the outward consequence encloses the person whose desire exceeded its bank.
The person who fears standing before the Lord restrains the self from desire, وَنَهَى النَّفْسَ عَنِ الْهَوَىٰ; this is the section's inner dam stated without the water metaphor.
The Garden is the abode of the person who builds the restraint in 79:40, completing the opposed outcomes of overflow and self-restraint.
Salih tells Thamud فَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَأَطِيعُونِ, calling them to put the protective restraint in place and to follow the messenger rather than the surge.
وَلَا تُطِيعُوا أَمْرَ الْمُسْرِفِينَ directly forbids following those who exceed measure, the social dam that could stop one offender from becoming a people's action.
Those whom 26:151 forbids obeying spread corruption in the land and do not repair it, specifying the public course into which the leaders' excess would direct the group.
Thamud are destroyed بِالطَّاغِيَةِ; the same root names both their overflow and the overwhelming thing by which it returns upon them.
The destroyed peoples are those الَّذِينَ طَغَوْا فِي الْبِلَادِ, extending Thamud's overflow into a pattern of transgression across lands.
They multiply corruption in those lands; this shows what the overflow of 89:11 produces before the returning punishment of 89:13.
God pours upon them, فَصَبَّ عَلَيْهِمْ, a scourge of punishment; the downward pouring answers the transgression described in 89:11-12 with the section's own fluid logic.

Thamud are shown guidance but prefer blindness, and the thunderbolt seizes them for what they earned; it explicitly stages their choice between the two disclosures given to the soul and its self-earned result.
Thamud call their companion and he undertakes the deed and hamstrings the camel; this is the fullest parallel to the single worst man rising while the people summon and support him.
The plural agents hamstring the camel and defy their Lord's command; attributing the deed to the people shows how the one man's surge becomes the community's act.
The plural فَعَقَرُوهَا again assigns the hamstringing to Thamud as a whole, then immediately announces the three-day boundary before the promise arrives.
The people collectively hamstring the camel and become regretful, preserving both the crowd's participation in one instigator's act and its recoil upon them.
Pharaoh makes his people light and they obey him; the ayah gives an exact leader-and-followers mechanism for the section's image of a people flowing after one transgressor.
When Pharaoh and his people provoke God, He takes vengeance and drowns them all; the obedient collective of 43:54 is engulfed together by the consequence.
Pharaoh pursues with his forces and the sea covers them; the leader's outward rush ends in the water overwhelming leader and followers together.
Pharaoh leads his people astray rather than guiding them, naming the misdirection that made the collective pursuit and drowning in 20:78 possible.

After rescue from danger at sea, people rebel on earth, but بِغْيُكُمْ عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِكُم; the watery scene and the statement that rebellion is against oneself precisely express the flood returning upon its source.
Pharaoh's people deny the signs, are taken for their sins, and are drowned; the ayah directly joins culpable denial to the water that engulfs its agents.
God seizes Pharaoh and his forces and casts them into the sea; the one who exalted himself and those who moved under him meet one shared watery end.
If provision were spread without limit, people would transgress in the earth, so God sends it down by measure; measured giving functions as a preventive bank against latent human overflow.
God gives good provision but warns وَلَا تَطْغَوْا فِيهِ lest wrath descend; remaining within the gift's limit is the dam, and crossing it causes the fall.
أَلَّا تَطْغَوْا فِي الْمِيزَانِ turns transgression into exceeding a balance, a precise Qur'anic formulation of crossing the section's limit.
The command to establish weight justly supplies the positive discipline that keeps the balance of 55:8 from being exceeded.
The ayah directly refuses to make الْمُتَّقِينَ كَالْفُجَّارِ, placing the protected and the morally bursting on the two opposed sides developed by the section.
وَإِنَّ الْفُجَّارَ لَفِي جَحِيمٍ carries fujur from an inward moral opening to the outward place that finally contains its agents.
Those who accept guidance receive more guidance and God gives them their taqwa, وَآتَاهُمْ تَقْوَاهُمْ; it closely parallels the soul being given knowledge of its protective capacity.
قُوا أَنفُسَكُمْ وَأَهْلِيكُمْ نَارًا uses the root's concrete force: place protection between selves and the feared fire, exactly the dictionary image behind taqwa.
Whoever is protected from the greed of his own soul, وَمَن يُوقَ شُحَّ نَفْسِهِ, succeeds; the barrier is internal, its pressure is the nafs, and its result is the success named around 91:9.
The repeated formula وَمَن يُوقَ شُحَّ نَفْسِهِ makes protection from one's own inward greed the condition of success, directly embodying the section's inner embankment.
The command not to obey one whose heart is heedless, who follows desire, and whose affair is excessive, فُرُطًا, closely restates Salih's attempt to stop obedience to overflowing leaders.
The command to cooperate in righteousness and taqwa but not in sin and aggression supplies a social barrier against a whole group flowing behind wrongdoing.
They did not restrain one another from wrongdoing they committed; this failure of mutual inhibition is the missing communal dam in the section's account of Thamud.
The condemned say they obeyed their leaders and great ones and were led away from the path; it is the explicit afterlife confession of a people who followed another's surge.
God calls these His limits and says not to approach them, then says He clarifies the signs so people may attain taqwa; taqwa here is visibly made by keeping a boundary.
تِلْكَ حُدُودُ اللَّهِ فَلَا تَعْتَدُوهَا names divine limits and forbids crossing them, directly articulating transgression as passage beyond a set line.
Whoever crosses God's limits has wronged himself; the violated boundary and the harm returning to its violator are joined in one sentence.

When Moses strikes the stone, twelve springs burst forth, فَانفَجَرَتْ مِنْهُ اثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ عَيْنًا; this is a direct Qur'anic instance of the physical water-surge from which the section derives fujur.
The ayah distinguishes stones from which rivers burst forth, لَمَا يَتَفَجَّرُ مِنْهُ الْأَنْهَارُ, preserving the root's concrete image of water breaking outward.
The opponents demand that the Prophet make a spring burst from the earth, تَفْجُرَ لَنَا مِنَ الْأَرْضِ يَنبُوعًا, a direct physical deployment of the fujur root.
Their next demand intensifies the scene into rivers made to burst abundantly through gardens, فَتُفَجِّرَ الْأَنْهَارَ خِلَالَهَا تَفْجِيرًا.
God causes a river to burst between the two gardens, وَفَجَّرْنَا خِلَالَهُمَا نَهَرًا; it retains the root's productive rather than sinful water sense.
Springs are made to burst among the gardens, وَفَجَّرْنَا فِيهَا مِنَ الْعُيُونِ, another concrete form of released water that shows the image is not inherently destructive.
God's servants make the spring flow forth abundantly, يُفَجِّرُونَهَا تَفْجِيرًا; the same bursting root is governed and life-giving rather than lawless.
When the seas are made to burst, وَإِذَا الْبِحَارُ فُجِّرَتْ, the root expands from a spring's opening to waters losing their cosmic bounds.
The gates of heaven are opened with pouring water; it supplies the water from above that meets the earth's burst springs in 54:12.
Noah is carried on planks and nails, completing the rescue side of the measured flood in 54:11-12 just as 69:11 joins overflow to being carried.
The oven gushes and Noah is told to load the ark; the sudden eruption of the Flood and the prepared vessel stage overflow beside protection.
Earth is commanded to swallow its water and sky to withhold, and the water subsides; divine command restores the banks after the flood has executed its task.
At the oven's eruption Noah is to put the pairs aboard; a bursting sign triggers the protective enclosure before engulfment.
The flood is sent upon Pharaoh's people as one of the detailed signs, yet they remain arrogant criminals; punitive water confronts the moral overflow before the final drowning.
Each people is seized for its own sin, with some drowned, and God did not wrong them but they wronged themselves; consequence is explicitly shaped by and returned to the offender.
God makes garments that protect from heat and armor that protects in battle, تَقِيكُم; these are tangible instances of putting something between a person and feared harm.
The condemned person tries to shield the face, يَتَّقِي بِوَجْهِهِ, from the evil punishment; the root's protective action appears at the moment when no real shield remains.
The people ask for a barrier against Gog and Magog because they spread corruption in the land; feared moral overflow is answered by a literal intervening structure.
Dhul-Qarnayn asks for strength to build a rampart between the people and the corrupters, stating the section's protective 'something between' in architectural form.
Iron blocks and molten copper are assembled into the barrier, making the protective limit a deliberately constructed restraint rather than a mere wish.
Gog and Magog can neither scale nor pierce the barrier; the feared surge is held on its far side.
Dhul-Qarnayn says the barrier will be levelled when God's promise comes; even a successful worldly restraint has an appointed boundary and end.
After the barrier's appointed end, the peoples surge into one another like waves, يَمُوجُ فِي بَعْضٍ; it literalizes the human flood released when the set is gone.
When Gog and Magog are opened, they stream down from every elevation; the removal of containment turns a multitude into a directed surge.
The soul persistently commands evil unless the Lord has mercy; it identifies the inward pressure for which the section's taqwa must serve as restraint.
David is told not to follow desire lest it lead him away from God's path; desire supplies the current, while the command supplies the bank against deviation from truth.
Believers are told not to follow desire lest they deviate from justice; this joins the section's 'inclining from truth' sense of fājir to failure to restrain desire.
Those who restrain anger, الْكَاظِمِينَ الْغَيْظَ, hold back an inward force before it spills into injury, a close nonlexical enactment of the inner dam.
Hell is a destination لِلطَّاغِينَ, so the place of return is assigned specifically to those who overflow the limit.
جَزَاءً وِفَاقًا calls that punishment a fitting recompense, confirming that the result in 78:22 corresponds to the transgression rather than arriving arbitrarily.
The record of the fujjār is in Sijjin; moral bursting is answered by a constricted register and destination.
Noah fears that the entrenched rejecters will produce only a fājir and intense unbeliever, presenting moral outbreak as something a corrupt community reproduces.
The faces covered by darkness are identified as الْكَفَرَةُ الْفَجَرَةُ, joining fujur to its disclosed final condition.
When the rock is struck, twelve springs gush, فَانبَجَسَتْ مِنْهُ اثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ عَيْنًا; a different verb stages the same controlled release of water as the section's root image.
God releases the two seas yet sets between them a barrier and forbidding partition; the ayah gives the section's intervening protection in a literal water scene.
The ayah asks who placed a barrier between the two seas, directly presenting the divinely set limit that prevents waters from becoming one unbounded mass.
Pharaoh proclaims himself the highest lord; this upward self-exaltation is the human analogue of water rising over everything and displays the taġā diagnosed in 79:17.
God seizes Pharaoh with the exemplary punishment of the last and first claim; his self-exalting overflow in 79:24 turns into the force that takes him.
Noah's son trusts a mountain to protect him, but there is no protector from God's command and the wave comes between them; the scene exposes a false barrier precisely when the flood rises.
Thamud object to following one human messenger, yet in 54:29 they call and follow their own companion into the crime; their stated fear of one-man leadership is reversed by their conduct.
The companion says مَا أَطْغَيْتُهُ, 'I did not make him transgress,' but that he was already far astray; it sets personal inward responsibility against the excuse that another supplied the overflow.
مَا زَاغَ الْبَصَرُ وَمَا طَغَى uses طغى for sight that does not go beyond its proper limit, a disciplined perceptual boundary rather than moral flood.
A wall is placed between believers and hypocrites, with mercy inside and punishment outside; the barrier protects one side while exposing the other to what it failed to prepare against.
Those who cross the measure are asked whether they think they will be raised, مَبْعُوثُونَ; the sinner's self-directed surge is answered by an unavoidable rising directed by God for judgment.
Barriers are placed before and behind the rejecters until they cannot see; it is a boundary that confines and blinds rather than the saving shelter represented by taqwa.
The righteous are in bliss, supplying the immediately adjacent opposite outcome to the fujjār's confinement in 82:14.
God leaves the hypocrites wandering blindly فِي طُغْيَانِهِمْ; their transgression becomes the element in which they remain carried about.
Revelation increases many of them in transgression and disbelief; what could have guided them instead swells the overflow already chosen within them.
Those who first refuse belief are left wandering in their transgression, making the chosen excess itself an ongoing condition rather than a single act.
The one God lets stray is left blindly wandering فِي طُغْيَانِهِمْ, again picturing transgression as a current that continues to carry its agents.
Those who do not expect the meeting with God are left wandering in their transgression; absence of feared return removes the restraint on the overflow.
Even removal of suffering would leave them obstinately wandering in their transgression, showing how a sustained inward flood resists an outward opening.
The warning vision and cursed tree only increase them in great transgression; resistance turns the warning itself into added volume for the surge.

The accused leaders answer that they had no authority over their followers, but the followers themselves were a transgressing people; the root joins collective overflow to responsibility within the crowd.
The transgressors are assigned an evil place of return, carrying the act of exceeding into its destination.

Successive peoples repeat the same charge against messengers because they are a transgressing people; the common overflow explains a pattern transmitted across generations without requiring one speaker to cause it.
The rejecters' speech is traced to their being a transgressing people, letting an inward excess break outward in their words.
After their garden is ruined, its owners confess إِنَّا كُنَّا طَاغِينَ; recognition comes when their plan to exclude the poor has already returned as deprivation.
The sea is parted to save Israel and Pharaoh's people are drowned before them; one water simultaneously becomes passage for the protected and closure over the pursuing oppressors.
Noah and those with him are saved in the ark while the deniers are drowned, repeating the section's conjunction of protective enclosure and punitive flood.
Pharaoh's people are drowned in the sea because they deny the signs and remain heedless, joining persistent refusal to engulfment.
Noah's party is saved in the ark and the deniers are drowned; the vessel is a concrete protection placed within the same water that destroys.
Drowning overtakes Pharaoh while he is pursuing in rebellion and aggression, bringing his moral excess and the returning water into one moment.
Pharaoh tries to uproot the people from the land, so he and all with him are drowned; the attempted sweeping-away recoils as literal engulfment.
Noah's people are drowned when they deny the messengers and are made a sign, another direct instance of denial answered through overwhelming water.
Noah and those with him are saved in the laden ship, presenting the protective side of the flood image.
Those remaining after the vessel of 26:119 are drowned, so the same scene separates the sheltered from those caught outside.
The Flood seizes Noah's people while they are wrongdoers, stating the external water and the moral condition together.
God saves Noah and his family from the great distress, foregrounding rescue from the impending overflow.
The others are drowned after Noah's rescue, completing the protected-versus-engulfed division begun in 37:76.
God seizes Pharaoh and his forces and casts them into the sea while he is blameworthy, linking collective following to a shared watery consequence.
The weak tell the arrogant that they followed them and ask whether they can avert any punishment; the leaders who drew the crowd cannot become its shield when consequence arrives.
The disbelievers invite believers to follow their path and falsely promise to carry their sins, showing the recruitment by which wrongdoing tries to gather a following.
They will carry their own burdens and burdens added for those they mislead, so the instigator's surge returns with responsibility for its social wake.
Those who mislead others bear their own burdens and part of the burdens of those misled, assigning consequence to the outward spread of their impulse.
The divine word becomes due against leaders and followers together, showing the common consequence of the transgressing crowd described in 37:30.
The leaders admit that they caused others to deviate because they themselves were deviant; the ayah traces the current from inward error to collective movement.
The weak tell the arrogant that they were followers and ask them to relieve part of the Fire; as in the flood image, following supplies no barrier from the shared outcome.
Noah says his people followed those whose wealth and children increased them only in loss, identifying the influential current they chose over the messenger.
The influential plotters lead many astray, preparing the social cause immediately before the drowning for sins in 71:25.
The 'garment of taqwa' makes protection wearable: an inward safeguard is imaged as the covering kept next to the body.
The angels ask God to protect the believers from evil deeds and say that whoever is protected that day receives mercy; the root joins moral harm, shelter, and final outcome.
God protects the believing man from the evils of Pharaoh's plot, making divine safeguarding an actual barrier against a transgressor's plan.
The people of the Garden taste no further death and God protects them from Hell's punishment, a completed form of the shelter sought by taqwa.
The blessed rejoice because their Lord has protected them from the punishment of Hell, explicitly naming the feared outcome kept outside the shelter.
God protects the righteous from the evil of that Day and grants brightness and joy, showing the eventual effect of the inner protection.
Obeying God and His messenger is joined to fearing God and having taqwa; it closely matches Salih's paired command to fear God and obey him.
God has tested the believers' hearts for taqwa, locating the protective quality in the inward faculty where the section places fujur and restraint.
A soul is told to look at what it has sent ahead while believers repeat the command to fear God; foresight of return supplies the restraint missing from the person who wants to sin forward in 75:5.
God shows the human being the two ascending ways, a nonlexical parallel to the soul being made aware of two opposed moral directions.
The human being is shown the way and may be grateful or ungrateful; disclosed alternatives remain a choice rather than a forced destiny.
The person who gives and has taqwa begins one branch of a paired moral sequence, corresponding to the restrained side disclosed to the soul.
God eases that person toward ease, showing how the protected choice of 92:5 becomes a continuing direction.
The opposite person withholds and considers himself self-sufficient, repeating the self-sufficiency that causes human overflow in 96:7.
That person is eased toward hardship, showing the contrary current produced by the unrestrained choice in 92:8-9.
Doing good is for oneself and doing evil is against oneself; the ayah states without water imagery the section's claim that the released harm turns back upon its source.
Corruption appears on land and sea through what people's hands have earned so that they taste some of it; human action becomes the environment that returns upon its makers.
An evil plot encloses only its own people, a compact nonlexical statement of the transgressor being caught by the force he released.
Calamity is tied to what people's hands have earned, supporting the section's reading of outward punishment as the return of inwardly chosen action.
Water is sent down in due measure and lodged in the earth, with God able to remove it; controlled measure and storage supply the calm opposite of destructive overflow.
God raises a messenger in every community to command worship and avoidance of tāghūt; divine dispatch counters the directing force of transgression.
God بعث Moses with signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs; this divinely directed sending confronts the ruler's self-directed overflow.
Moses is commanded to go to Pharaoh because he has transgressed, an earlier direct formulation of the mission and diagnosis quoted from 79:17.
Moses and Aaron together are sent to Pharaoh because he has transgressed, placing a commissioned pair against one ruler's excess.
They fear that Pharaoh may hasten against them or transgress further, showing taġā as the feared crossing their mission must confront.
Pharaoh denies and disobeys after Moses' offer, showing the first outward break produced by the overflow diagnosed in 79:17.
He turns away striving, converting the inward refusal of 79:21 into directed movement.
He gathers people and calls out, the leader's act that turns his own surge into a public current.
Pharaoh is described as exalted in the land and among the excessive; height and excess combine in the ruler who later leads his people into the sea.
Pharaoh is called high and one of the excessive, linking self-elevation to the boundary-crossing that ends in drowning.
The excessive are named companions of the Fire, giving those who exceed measure a final encompassing destination.

The command not to follow Satan's steps because he commands indecency, followed by God's purification, plausibly maps the small successive steps by which an outward moral surge grows; the water link remains implicit.

Those with taqwa remember when a satanic impulse touches them and then see clearly; this plausibly depicts the protective intervention before an impulse becomes a current, though no barrier image is stated.
As drowning overtakes Pharaoh, he is confronted with his earlier disobedience and corruption; the ayah identifies the moral current whose watery return is staged in 10:90.

Pharaoh and his forces act arrogantly in the land and deny their return to God; this supplies both the leader-and-company surge and the rejected boundary immediately before they are cast into the sea in 28:40.
A single blast leaves Thamud like the dry fragments of an enclosure; one collective stroke answers the collective crime set in motion by their companion in 54:29.
The punishment seizes Thamud after their collective hamstringing in 26:157, making the outward consequence the immediate return of the act.
The earthquake seizes Thamud after the people's defiant hamstringing in 7:77; their outward surge ends with the whole settlement brought low.
The blast seizes the wrongdoers after the three-day limit announced in 11:65, completing the movement from crossed boundary to collective consequence.
Nine factions in Salih's city spread corruption and do not repair; this is a precise social form of several instigators keeping a people in motion toward excess.
The corrupt faction plots, while God answers their plot without their awareness; the released scheme already contains the counter-movement that will return on them.
The result of the plot is the destruction of the plotters and their people together, joining initiating leaders and the surrounding collective in one consequence.
Moses offers to guide Pharaoh to his Lord so that he may fear; this supplies the fear-based restraint paired with purification in 79:18 and opposed to Pharaoh's overflow in 79:17.
The declaration that the return is to the Lord places an unavoidable outer limit immediately after the human being's self-sufficient transgression in 96:6-7.
The final command not to obey the transgressor, but to prostrate and draw near, gives the social and devotional restraint that answers the self-sufficient overflow introduced in 96:6-7.
The command to guard oneself against the Fire uses taqwa in the section's concrete sense of placing protection between the self and a feared consequence.
God teaches the making of armor to protect people from their violence; a manufactured layer between the body and feared harm is a literal counterpart to the section's definition of taqwa.
The person of greatest taqwa is kept away from the blazing Fire, showing the protective disposition accomplishing an actual separation from the feared thing.
God saves those with taqwa so that evil does not touch them; the inward protection becomes an outwardly effective shelter at the result.
God rescues those with taqwa and leaves the wrongdoers kneeling in Hell, using the protective quality to draw the final boundary between two outcomes.
The prayer to be protected from the punishment of the Fire, وَقِنَا عَذَابَ النَّارِ, states the root's sheltering action and its feared object directly.
Believers ask God to forgive them and protect them from the punishment of the Fire; moral repair and the sought protective barrier are joined.
Those who reflect ask to be protected from the punishment of the Fire, another explicit use of the root for shelter from what is feared.
The people of the Garden say God favored them and protected them from the scorching punishment; it names the completed shelter whose inward form is taqwa.
Noah's ark moves through mountain-like waves while he calls his separated son; it supplies the engulfing water and the attempted rescue immediately before the failed refuge of 11:43.
Once settled in the ark, Noah is told to praise God for rescue from the wrongdoing people; the enclosure is explicitly experienced as protection from both flood and collective wrongdoing.
The ark sails under God's watch as recompense for the rejected messenger, completing the protective side of the converging waters in 54:11-13.
God saves Moses and everyone with him, placing the protected company on one side of the divided sea scene.
The others are drowned after Moses' party is saved in 26:65; following the transgressing ruler places the whole company on the engulfed side.
Moses is told to leave the sea parted because Pharaoh's army is destined to drown; the water is held open as refuge and poised to close over the pursuing surge.
The evils the people committed strike them, and what they mocked surrounds them; consequence is figured as their own released action returning to enclose them.
Those who were followed disown their followers when punishment is seen and all ties are cut; the leaders who carried the crowd cannot become a shelter from its destination.
The followers long for a return so they could disown their leaders, but their deeds become regrets and they cannot leave the Fire; the social current has hardened into an inescapable outcome.
Leaders and followers share the punishment after their dispute over who caused the transgression; the collective that flowed together is contained together by its result.
Pharaoh and his circle are made leaders calling toward the Fire, an exact statement of one ruling current directing followers into the punishment it invites.
A people are cursed because they disobeyed and habitually transgressed; it supplies the repeated overflow whose social mechanism is their failure to restrain one another in 5:79.
Believers are warned against a trial that will not strike only the wrongdoers among them; the ayah makes failure to contain wrongdoing a danger that spreads beyond its first agents.
Whoever disobeys God and His messenger and crosses His limits is made to enter the Fire, directly joining boundary violation to its enclosing consequence.
The faithful are described as forbidding wrong and guarding God's limits; they perform the communal and boundary-keeping work missing in Thamud's collective surge.
Right guidance is distinguished from error, and rejecting tāghūt while believing in God is likened to grasping an unbreakable handhold; moral choice and a protective attachment meet in one image.
A violent wind and waves from every side drive voyagers to sincere prayer; this is the containing sea crisis from which 10:23 says they emerge only to overflow again on land.
God can return people to the sea, send a violent wind, and drown them for disbelief, after which they find no protector; returning water and failed shelter are explicitly joined.
Salih's mission immediately divides Thamud into two contending parties, staging the people's choice between the opposed directions disclosed to the soul.
Salih asks why they hasten evil before good instead of seeking forgiveness; the people actively call forward the consequence that their excess will bring back upon them.
The water is divided between Thamud and the camel in appointed shares; the crime that follows is thus a violation of a measured water boundary, not an unmarked act.
Salih presents the she-camel as a sign, grants her access to God's land, and sets the boundary not to harm her lest punishment seize them.
Salih tells his people to leave God's camel to feed and not touch her with harm lest a near punishment take them; the protective prohibition clearly marks the bank they cross.
Salih assigns the camel one share of drink and the people another on known days, giving the Thamud story a precise measured-water limit.
He forbids touching the camel with harm lest a tremendous day's punishment seize them; the warning tries to place a restraint before the collective act of 26:157.
Noah's people are called especially unjust and transgressing; the moral overflow belongs specifically to the people later remembered through the engulfing Flood.
Satan tells his followers that he had no coercive authority, only invited them, and tells them to blame themselves; it sharply limits the leader excuse while preserving the fact of a followed call.
The person who takes desire as a god is left with sealed hearing and heart and a covering over sight; unrestrained desire produces enclosing barriers that blind rather than protect.
A barrier stands behind the dead until the day they are raised; unlike the chosen moral restraint of taqwa, this boundary is imposed after choice has ended and cannot be crossed back for repair.
The resurrected ask who raised them from their resting place; their unavoidable God-directed rising reverses the self-directed launch of Thamud's worst man.
The rejecters are asked who could protect them from painful punishment; the question exposes the absence of any true barrier once the feared result has arrived.
The challenge to consider God's punishment and warnings marks the interpretive turn from the companion's crime in 54:29 to the collective devastation in 54:31.
The arrogant faction openly rejects what Salih brings, fixing the collective choice that immediately becomes the hamstringing in 7:77.
Thamud deny the warnings, supplying the people's initial refusal before their dispute about whom to follow and their call to the offending companion.
The passage asks the reader to consider the person who forbids another; it begins to show the concrete conduct into which self-sufficient transgression in 96:6-7 breaks outward.
The object of the prohibition is a servant at prayer, making the transgressor's outward act an attempt to obstruct another person's worship.
Denial and turning away further specify the conduct of the self-sufficient transgressor before the final command not to obey him.
The command to guard against the Fire prepared for rejecters uses taqwa directly as protection from a named feared outcome.
The evils people earned become visible to them and the thing they mocked surrounds them; the released wrong returns as an encompassing condition.
Their evil deeds appear and what they mocked encloses them, repeating the section's claim that wrongdoing supplies the form of its own returning consequence.
The followers ask that their leaders receive doubled punishment and a great curse; it is their final recognition of the added responsibility borne by those who directed the crowd.
The arrogant answer their former followers that all are in the Fire and God has judged between His servants; neither status nor leadership can hold back the shared result.
A companion led the speaker away from remembrance after it had come; a personal relationship becomes the channel through which another's deviation carries someone with it.
The command not to obey a contemptible habitual swearer begins a detailed portrait of the sort of influential offender whose impulse must not be followed.
That figure is a hinderer of good, a transgressor, and a sinner; the description supplies the crossed limit and outward harm behind the non-obedience command of 68:10.
The Prophet is told not to obey any sinner or obstinate rejecter among them, another direct social restraint against being drawn into another's moral surge.
The paired command to have taqwa and not obey the rejecters closely parallels Salih's call to fear God and refuse the commands of the excessive.
Moses is warned not to let one who denies the Hour and follows desire turn him from it, lest he perish; resistance to another's desire-driven pull is made a protective act.
A community is to call to good and forbid wrong, giving the positive institutional form of a social dam against spreading misconduct.
The seaside community transgresses the Sabbath boundary when the fish appear conspicuously on the forbidden day; desire, water, and a tested limit meet in one concrete scene.
People may eat and drink but must not exceed; bodily intake is given a clear bank, and excess rather than the provision itself is condemned.
God raises Moses and Aaron with signs against Pharaoh and his chiefs; divinely directed sending confronts the arrogant criminal leadership.
When the first promise arrives, God sends formidable servants against the corrupters; a directed force comes back upon those whose own power had overflowed.
God can send punishment from above or below and can divide people into factions that taste one another's violence; directed consequence and social contagion are held together.
The believing parents are feared to be overborne by their child's transgression and disbelief; the ayah uses overflow for a pressure capable of carrying close others with it.
The allies of tāghūt lead their followers from light into darkness and finally the Fire; false authority is presented as a directing current toward enclosure.
God's seizure of wrongdoing towns is painful and severe; the statement generalizes the narrative pattern in which a settlement's sustained wrongdoing returns as a collective taking.
When distress strikes at sea, every trusted power disappears except God, but after rescue to land people turn away; removal of danger also removes their temporary restraint.

Those rescued to land are asked whether they feel secure from being swallowed or struck by a storm, and are told they would find no guardian; safety outside the sea is not an absolute barrier from consequence.
People in a ship call sincerely upon God, then associate others once delivered to land; like 10:22-23, constraint at sea gives way to moral overflow after rescue.
Their post-rescue ingratitude is allowed a brief enjoyment before knowledge arrives, placing a temporal boundary around the renewed excess of 29:65.
When waves cover voyagers like canopies they call sincerely upon God, but after rescue responses divide; engulfing water reveals restraint that some preserve and others betray.
Whoever responds to the messengers with taqwa and repair will have no fear or grief; protection and active repair are paired against the corruption produced by excess.
The best provision for the journey is called taqwa; the protective quality is imagined as something carried in advance rather than sought only after danger arrives.
Whoever earns a sin earns it only against himself, a direct non-water formulation of the section's claim that released wrongdoing turns upon its source.
